title: Pushing progression and avoiding plateaus using evolving rep ranges
summary: NH explains why evolving rep ranges push plateaus away better than static ones: you can repeat a weight while total tonnage keeps rising. When you do stall, widen the range, use smaller weight jumps, add or remove a set, or add another lift that carries over. Deliberate sandbagging on lifts that feed other lifts is fine.
claims: Your job is to see plateaus coming and push them ahead of you; slow steady progress beats repeatedly hitting a wall even if the latter seems faster
Evolving rep ranges progress more slowly than static ones but are the best tool for avoiding plateaus
Static rep ranges are fine for novices to a point; then move toward evolving ranges
With 3x5 you add weight once you hit 5 reps on all 3 sets; if you fail you repeat or deload, which leaves few options
A narrow range like 3x3-5 behaves mostly like a static range; the wider the range, the more flexibility and the fewer static benefits
Ranges that are too wide (e.g. 3x3-20) are poorly built because it would take months to earn a weight increase
Evolving ranges let you repeat the same weight across sessions while tonnage keeps rising (e.g. 4-4-3, then 5-4-3, then 5-5-4)
Evolving ranges turn sandbagging into productive progression
The final form is evolving sets plus evolving reps, but beginners should keep sets fixed because evolving both is much more complex
When stalled within an evolving range, first try widening the range so tonnage can keep climbing at the same weight
If you stall, your weight jumps may be too big; halve them (e.g. 2.5-5 lb per side instead of 10)
Add a set to break through a plateau; alternatively drop a set to push more reps on the rest, then add it back
If no other lift in your program carries over to the stalled lift, add one, as back-off sets or on another day
Four lifts for the same muscle in one day, or 12 exercises and 25-55 weekly sets, is likely too much junk volume
He rarely uses ranges like 5 sets of 20-25 because they're wasteful
Range width signals intent: narrow means you expect quick weight jumps, wide means you don't
Junk volume is bad only when it replaces quality tonnage or takes time from other body parts
Unintentional sandbagging is bad; deliberate sandbagging on lifts that feed others is good, and he has many such lifts in his program
You can slow progression to a crawl if that serves your goals; it's not a race
